fetched_contents.text: Characteristics and Recommendations for the Virtual Role Model Visit — Based on a Literature Review Abstract In recent years, several role-modelling initiatives have been testing and exploring the use of digital technologies to facilitate young people’s encounters with role models in the science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields. The aim of this article is twofold. Firstly, through a literature review, the article aims to provide an overview of how digital technologies have been used to facilitate the students’ encounters with STEM role models. The literature review shows how the use of digital technologies (1) enables scaling so that more young people can have access to role models, (2) enables the role models to show authentic work tasks and environments through virtual field visits, allowing pupils to closely examine the work processes in production companies, the laboratory, or in geographically remote locations, (3) opens up new opportunities for young people to interact and become involved, both through synchronous and asynchronous communication. The second aim of the article is to present, based on the knowledge gained from the literature study, a framework of eleven recommendations for the design of future virtual role model visits. Keywords: Role model, Virtual role model, Literature review, STEM, Learning design Introduction The use of role models is a well-known tool for inspiring youth in the science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) fields, as the pupils’ encounters with workplace professionals have been shown to potentially strengthen young people’s motivation to pursue a STEM education (MacCallum & Beltman, 2002; Wentzel & Brophy, 2014). In recent years, several role-modelling initiatives (see the “What Characterises Virtual Role Model Visits?” section) have been testing and exploring the use of digital technologies to facilitate young people’s encounters with role models. The motivations for using digital technologies to support the role model visit include reaching schools in sparsely populated areas, ensuring access to a diversity of role models, saving resources in terms of transport, and planning and scaling the role model visit to reach more pupils and make better use of the role models’ time (Adedokun et al., 2012; Dawson et al., 2015; O’Donoghue, 2020; Schinske et al., 2016; Ware & Stein, 2013). Another motivation for working with digital technologies to facilitate young people’s interaction with role models is that their interaction with the “real world”, including role models, can be developed and improved by technology. There are different perspectives and therefore definitions of what a role model is. In this context, we have used a broad understanding of the term: “They [role models] may provide an example of someone who has succeeded outside a traditional societal role, has overcome a particular social or physical disadvantage, has gained status in our society or who possesses particular skills, knowledge or personal attributes that are seen to be desirable in a particular setting” (MacCallum & Beltman, 2002, p. 24). In this way, a role model acts as an example of a person who possesses qualities that an individual imitates as motivation for future achievements (Ware & Stein, 2013). This broad understanding of the role model as a notion will be the basis of this article, as the understanding can cover the many perspectives of a virtual role model visit identified in the literature review. This article has two purposes. Firstly, through a literature review, the article aims to provide an overview of how digital technologies have been used to facilitate the students’ encounters with STEM role models. Based on the knowledge gained from the literature study, eleven recommendations for the design of future virtual role model visits are then formulated from a learning design perspective. Method This literature review takes the form of a narrative review (Bryman, 2016) with an aim to provide an overview and an interpretation of how digital technologies have been used to to facilitate young people’s encounters with role models. An initial exploratory search in Google Scholar and a university library catalogue was conducted to identify relevant search keywords. The initial exploratory search also identified two general approaches to creating a connection between young people and role models: (1) field trips, where students visit e.g., a university or a field site, and (2) visits, where the role model visits the students at educational institutions (Adedokun et al., 2015). This overall distinction is evident in physical field trips and visits, and it was considered important that studies of both types of visits were included in the review. Search keywords included those related to the role model visit (e.g., role model or outreach program) and keywords for technology supported visit (e.g., virtual expedition, online visit, or video conference). In this review, we searched Scopus, Academic Search Premier and ERIC database. No search restrictions were placed upon publication year, investigated individuals’ level of education or age. The original search results returned 331 research articles. In the next step, we reviewed the abstract and full text of the selected articles to confirm whether the studies were (1) empirical, (2) related to the concept of role model, (3) using digital technology to facilitate the role model visit, (4) conducted in context of a STEM discipline. fetched_contents.text: Pros and Cons of Synchronous, Asynchronous, and Hybrid Learning As virtual classroom offerings become more popular among learners—a recent Rand study found 1 in 5 K-12 schools intend to provide online-only options—many school districts and institutions find themselves debating about synchronous vs. asynchronous education, hybrid learning styles, and the various modalities available with teaching online. Gone are the days when virtual classroom platforms were essentially web conferencing for education. Now, online classroom platforms are far more robust and provide educators and learners with numerous ways to deepen the academic experience, as well as provide true accessibility for more learners. As Ellen Li, a co-founder of Princeton’s Disability Collective, tells the Chronicle of Higher Education, “Providing no online option is equivalent to denying disabled students, and teachers, any place in [schools].” With advancing technologies, the pros and cons of synchronous, asynchronous, and hybrid learning for online classrooms are becoming more well-defined. What is synchronous online learning? Synchronous online learning mainly categorizes the nature by which instructors and learners interact—keeping those communications occurring in real time. Much like in-classroom settings, synchronous online learning can occur either lecture-style (one-way) or interpersonally (two-way) at a specified time where all participants are present virtually. Pros of synchronous online learning A clear benefit of synchronous online learning is the ability for learners to have input into the information being dispersed. This can be via questions, clarifications, group discussions, and more. The nature of synchronous online learning has evolved, as well. Virtual classroom platforms now provide enhanced features like breakout rooms, self-paced video viewing, and much more that allow students to be present, engage in real-time, and retain a degree of learning autonomy. Additionally, as Matt Marino points out in his editorial for Education Articles, synchronous online learning provides structure and routine for students, which can also benefit their comprehension success. This routine can also benefit educators who are teaching online using modified versions of previous lesson plans. Cons of synchronous online learning While communicating in real-time has obvious advantages for educators and learners, there are some drawbacks. Much like a brick-and-mortar classroom, synchronous online learning can only happen at predetermined times, so if there is any sort of scheduling conflict, that learning opportunity is missed. Additionally, if relying solely on real-time communication without asynchronous resources like study sheets and recordings, students may fall behind and miss pieces of information or struggle to take notes and participate fully. Much like in-classroom settings, learners who are shy may also have difficulty providing feedback, whether in the form of questions for clarification or requesting an instructor repeat themselves or slow down. What is asynchronous online learning? Asynchronous online learning, by comparison, occurs in staggered timelines. An instructor may post a lecture or a reading assignment first thing in the morning and students may have a predetermined amount of time (for instance, 24 hours) to engage with the piece at a time that works best in their schedule. Pros of asynchronous online learning A notable advantage of asynchronous online learning is the flexibility it allows both educators and learners. In the debate of synchronous vs. asynchronous online learning, students with nontraditional schedules (like youth who are performers or athletes), as well as nontraditional higher education students who have full-time jobs, family responsibilities, and other commitments can benefit greatly from this flexible scheduling. Another valuable reason asynchronous online learning is so popular is that it eliminates the barrier of time zones. As eLearning Industry explains, “Learners are no longer limited to options available in their region and country, but can enroll in a course from a [school] in another part of the world with just a few clicks.” While virtual classrooms theoretically remove the need for physical proximity, a student on a different continent would struggle to consistently attend a synchronous course which requires them to be up in the middle of the night. Asynchronous online learning allows anyone, anywhere to participate. Cons of asynchronous online learning While flexibility is a very enticing feature, strictly asynchronous online learning can reduce a learner’s ability to engage, build peer relationships, and work collaboratively. Group projects are still largely solo endeavors in a strictly asynchronous workspace, further discussion of course topics is stunted and takes longer to evolve due to large gaps between various users’ input. Additionally, pre-recorded lectures or pre-defined assignments don’t allow for students to ask questions or get clarifications in real-time so learners are left to await additional asynchronous communication—via email, LMS messaging, texting, etc.—before starting on their assignment. What does hybrid learning look like with a virtual classroom? While the debate still rages on for some educators on the value of synchronous vs. asynchronous online learning, many have realized that hybrid learning styles allow them to leverage the benefits of each to the advantage of the educator and learners. Vargas and Yessenia Gamez Texas A&M University-College Station Technology improvements have opened an avenue for online mentoring and coaching for in-service teachers. Providing effective mentoring and coaching online is a viable alternative when traditional methods are unfeasible. A systematic review was conducted to understand virtual mentoring and coaching (VMC) over the last two decades. Findings from 15 studies that met full-text level criteria indicated that VMC is an effective method to support teachers. However, due to variability in the studies' design of VMC implementation, it is not easy to decipher what specific features of VMC make VMC effective. In developing future VMC opportunities, there is a need to understand effective features to maximize teacher learning. Nevertheless, this review has significant implications regarding VMC developments for in-service teachers. Keywords: mentoring, coaching, online, virtual, professional development, emergent bilinguals, in-service teachers In the United States, classrooms have become more ethnically and racially diverse in recent decades (U.S. Census Bureau, 2019). Researchers, policymakers, and teachers are battling ways to address emergent bilinguals' (EBs: refers to students who come from non-English speaking backgrounds) needs as many struggle academically. According to the statistics, EBs represent a susceptible population of learners across all major subject areas in education (National Center for Educational Statistics, 2019). This can be attributed to many factors such as EBs being tasked with learning content and language simultaneously (Gupta, 2019; Villegas, 2018). This, coupled with low performance in national standardized assessments, influences policies such as the Every Student Succeeds Act, emphasizing a commitment to equal opportunity for specifically disadvantaged and high needs students in the United States (U.S. Department of Education, 2015). In education, equity refers to providing all students with "the opportunity to receive a fair, equitable, and high-quality education [that closes] educational achievement gaps" (U.S. Department of Education, 2015, Sec. 1001. Statement of Purpose); thus, the Every Student Succeeds Act mandated that each state's educational plan demonstrate the adoption of English language proficiency standards that (a) recognize four domains such as "speaking, listening, reading, and writing"; (b) address EBs' various proficiency levels; and most importantly (c) are aligned with state academic standards (U.S. Department of Education, 2015, p. 25). However, while bilingual or English as a Second Language (ESL) teachers are aware of proficiency levels across the four domains, the familiarity between proficiency levels and content standards is less likely to be evident because it requires knowledge of various sets of content standards (Lee, 2018). Therefore, the Every Student Succeeds Act has mandated the effective advancement of Literature Reviews in Education and Human Services Fall 2022, Volume 1, Issue 2, 32-55 VIRTUAL MENTORING AND COACHING 33 professional development (PD) needed to improve teachers of EBs instruction (U.S. Department of Education, 2015). Effective teacher PD supports teachers in advancing complex and unique skills necessary to reach various learners. Darling-Hammond et al. (2017) defined effective PD as "professional learning that results in changes in teacher practices and improvements in student learning outcomes" (p. 5). Technological advances from unique recent challenges have amplified interest in virtual professional development (VPD). The challenges created by COVID-19 for educators across the country were unpredictable and forced adaptation through virtual means. Student learning was not the only element pushed into online platforms; professional training was as well. Although PD can help teach various pedagogical skills, applying that knowledge in everyday instruction does not always occur (Holmes et al., 2005; Knight, 2009, as cited in Gilbert, 2018). One way to guide teachers of EBs in the implementation of new techniques in their everyday instruction would be through tailored support. However, challenges of onsite assistance have led researchers and PD providers to investigate how technology could foster individualized support (Carmouche et al., 2018; Pianta et al., 2008). Online individualized support has been commonly referred to in the literature as web-based, online, or e- mentoring/coaching. To remain consistent throughout this article, we use the term virtual mentoring and coaching (VMC), a term previously first coined in the literature by Irby (2015). VMC allows mentors/coaches and mentees to interact with minimal constraints due to time, availability, and geography (Bang, 2013; Vernon- Feagans et al., 2015). Most importantly, VMC can be more efficient in feasibility and accessibility without negatively impacting its effectiveness (Gilbert, 2018). Ultimately, we want to support teachers' professional growth regardless of the method used to deliver quality PD. Pedagogical Practices As mentioned earlier, equitable education refers to a fair and high-quality education that results in minimizing achievement gaps for disadvantaged and high-needs students (U.S. Department of Education, 2015). Research shows that "higher-quality instruction is positively correlated with EBs outcomes" (Solari et al., 2016, p. 1061). Therefore, a teacher's ability to deliver fair, equitable and high-quality instruction that addresses EBs' academic, linguistic, and cultural needs should encompass their skill to present content through various pedagogical practices. Hybrid projects in virtual role model visits combine synchronous and asynchronous interaction to balance flexibility, immediacy, and reflection. The advantage of flexibility is central: asynchronous components reduce scheduling burden by allowing participants to engage at their own pace, which is especially helpful when participants have nontraditional schedules, family responsibilities, or geographic constraints [N2-F2]. This is consistent with the broader hybrid-learning logic in virtual classrooms, where asynchronous learning allows anyone, anywhere to participate and eliminates the barrier of time zones [N2-F2]. In the virtual role model visit context, that flexibility supports wider access, especially for students in sparsely populated areas or those unable to attend a live visit in person [N1-F1].

Real-time interaction supports immediacy and rapport by enabling direct communication, questions, clarifications, and group discussions during a visit [N2-F2]. In the literature review on virtual role model visits, the use of digital technologies is explicitly tied to enabling authentic work tasks and environments and to allowing pupils to closely examine the work processes of role models through virtual field visits, which suggests that synchronous interaction helps maintain the presence and authenticity of the role model experience [N1-F1]. The same source also notes that digital technologies can improve the interaction with the “real world,” including role models, by technology-mediated engagement [N1-F1]. This aligns with the general advantage of synchronous learning in hybrid settings: it provides structure, routine, and opportunities for input and engagement that asynchronous-only learning can lack [N2-F2].

Asynchronous components also reduce scheduling burden and enable reflection. Asynchronous learning eliminates the need for all participants to be present at the same time, which makes it easier to accommodate multiple participants across different time zones or conflicting schedules [N2-F2]. At the same time, asynchronous formats allow learners to review material, process it, and reflect more deeply before engaging further [N2-F2]. In the virtual role model visit literature, this is relevant because role models can show authentic work tasks and environments through virtual field visits, and students can interact through synchronous and asynchronous communication [N1-F1]. The evidence here suggests that asynchronous interaction complements the role model visit by giving participants time to absorb the content and later reflect on it, rather than trying to absorb everything in one session [N1-F1].

Overall, the hybrid advantage for virtual role model visits is a balance: flexibility and accessibility from asynchronous components, immediacy and rapport from synchronous interaction, and reflective processing that asynchronous design supports [N2-F2][N1-F1].

Hybrid virtual role model visits introduce several limitations and tradeoffs, particularly around fragmentation, technical barriers, and changes in participant workload and attention. One key concern is potential fragmentation or confusion from mixed modes. The general hybrid-learning literature notes that strictly asynchronous learning can reduce a learner’s ability to engage, build peer relationships, and work collaboratively, and that group projects become largely solo endeavors in asynchronous spaces [N2-F2]. In the virtual role model visit context, this could translate into participants being pulled between different interaction modes without clear boundaries, which may make the visit feel disjointed or harder to follow [N2-F2]. The literature review on virtual role model visits also emphasizes that digital technologies enable interaction through both synchronous and asynchronous communication, which implies that the hybrid design must be carefully structured to avoid confusion about what is expected when [N1-F1].

Technical barriers to seamless switching or integration are another important tradeoff. The hybrid-learning evidence notes that hybrid models combine real-time and at-your-own-pace experiences, but it also highlights that scheduling conflicts and reliance on real-time communication without asynchronous resources can create gaps and missed learning opportunities [N2-F2]. In virtual role model visits, this could mean that participants may struggle with technical transitions between modes, such as moving from a live Q&A session to a recorded follow-up or asynchronous reflection task, especially if the platform or workflow is not well integrated [N2-F2]. The logistics and implementation evidence from the broader hybrid-learning context also points to the need for structured organization and clear planning when mixing live and digital learning [N4-R1]. While that evidence is broader, it supports the idea that technical integration can be a bottleneck rather than a straightforward benefit [N4-R1].

Participant workload and attention may change in ways that are not always positive. The hybrid-learning literature states that synchronous learning can only happen at predetermined times, so scheduling conflicts may cause participants to miss opportunities [N2-F2]. Asynchronous learning, while flexible, can also increase workload because participants may need to manage more self-directed work, review materials, and wait for clarifications through email or messaging [N2-F2]. In the virtual role model visit context, this means participants may face a heavier cognitive load: they must attend a live session, then later process and reflect on the content asynchronously, while also managing the extra work of staying on task and keeping up with the visit’s requirements [N2-F2]. The evidence on virtual role model visits also notes that the role model visit can be scaled and saved resources in terms of transport, but this does not automatically eliminate the burden on participants [N1-F1].

In short, the main tradeoffs are fragmentation/confusion from mixed modes, technical barriers to smooth integration, and increased workload or attention demands that may offset some of the flexibility gains [N2-F2][N4-R1].

Context-specific evidence for role model visits in virtual settings points to several education and coaching settings that are particularly suited to this model. The most direct evidence comes from virtual mentoring and coaching literature, which frames VMC as an effective method to support teachers and other professionals in professional development [N5-F3]. In this context, virtual mentoring and coaching are described as a viable alternative when traditional methods are unfeasible, and they can provide individualized support through web-based, online, or e-mentoring/coaching formats [N5-F3]. The literature review on virtual mentoring and coaching also emphasizes that structured mentoring programs encourage teamwork, leadership, and research, helping teachers enhance their approaches and remain effective [N5-R5]. This suggests that coaching and mentoring settings are well suited to virtual role model visits, especially when the goal is professional growth, guidance, and support [N5-F3][N5-R5].

The evidence also supports virtual role model visits in STEM education and broader youth engagement settings. The virtual role model visit literature review specifically focuses on students’ encounters with STEM role models and notes that digital technologies enable scaling so that more young people can have access to role models, and that role models can show authentic work tasks and environments through virtual field visits [N1-F1]. It also states that virtual role model visits can be used to connect young people with workplace professionals, which is consistent with coaching and mentoring contexts where role models provide examples of success and guidance [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The same source notes that the motivation for using digital technologies includes reaching schools in sparsely populated areas, ensuring access to a diversity of role models, saving resources in transport, and planning/scaling the visit [N1-F1]. These factors make virtual role model visits especially suitable for education settings with geographic, resource, or access constraints.

On outcomes supported by the evidence, the literature is broad but encouraging. The virtual mentoring and coaching review finds that VMC is an effective method to support teachers [N5-F3]. The virtual role model visit literature review finds that digital technologies can strengthen young people’s motivation to pursue a STEM education by exposing them to workplace professionals and authentic work environments [N1-F1]. It also reports that the review identified 16 empirical studies, showing that the evidence base is substantive but still evolving [N1-F1]. In addition, the review emphasizes that VMC can be efficient in feasibility and accessibility without negatively impacting its effectiveness [N5-F3]. This suggests that the evidence supports improved access, professional growth, and motivation, especially for teachers and students in STEM-related contexts [N1-F1][N5-F3].

Evidence gaps and exceptions should be noted. First, the virtual mentoring and coaching evidence indicates variability in VMC implementation design, making it difficult to pinpoint which specific features make it effective [N5-F3]. Similarly, the virtual role model visit literature review emphasizes that the review is narrative and that studies were excluded if digital technology was only mentioned briefly rather than as a communication tool between role models and young people [N1-F1]. This means the evidence is promising, but not yet fully standardized or universally replicable across all virtual role model visit designs. Second, the evidence is stronger in STEM education and professional development contexts than in all coaching or role model settings, so generalization should be cautious [N1-F1][N5-F3]. Overall, the context-specific evidence supports virtual role model visits in education, coaching, and professional development settings, especially when the goal is access, motivation, and support [N1-F1][N5-F3].

The model is especially well suited to contexts where participants have varying schedules, geographic constraints, or learning needs that benefit from both direct engagement and self-paced processing [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## Key features and advantages of hybrid projects in virtual role model visits

Hybrid projects in virtual role model visits combine **synchronous and asynchronous interactions** into a single design, balancing the strengths of each mode. The core features of the hybrid model are:  
- a **structured combination of real-time and self-paced experiences** [N1-F1],  
- **synchronous interaction** for direct engagement with role models, such as live Q&A, field visits, or real-time exchanges [N1-F1], and  
- **asynchronous interaction** for reflection, preparation, or follow-up [N1-F1].  

### 1) How the hybrid model is structured in practice

The hybrid project model is not a random mix of synchronous and asynchronous elements; it is a deliberate design choice. The virtual role model visit literature explicitly states that future visits should combine the use of **synchronous and asynchronous communication** [N1-R1], and the same source emphasizes that digital technologies enable interaction through both synchronous and asynchronous communication [N1-F1]. This suggests a coordinated structure where each mode serves a different purpose.

In practice, the model typically works like this:  
- **Synchronous components** are used for the core encounter with the role model, including live sessions where participants can ask questions, observe work environments, or experience the role model’s authentic tasks [N1-F1].  
- **Asynchronous components** support reflection, discussion, or follow-up after the live interaction, allowing participants to process the visit at their own pace [N1-F1].  
- The broader hybrid-learning literature supports this structure by distinguishing synchronous learning as real-time and asynchronous learning as staggered timelines, with hybrid learning combining both [N2-F2].  

### 2) Who initiates each interaction and under what conditions

The evidence suggests a pattern of **role model-led live interaction paired with participant-led asynchronous follow-up** [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The virtual role model visit literature implies that role models are typically the ones initiating the encounter, while students or participants later initiate follow-up, reflection, or discussion [N1-F1]. The broader hybrid-learning evidence also notes that asynchronous learning can be initiated by instructors by posting materials, and learners can engage at their own pace [N2-F2]. In the virtual role model visit context, this likely means the role model initiates the live session, while participants may later initiate asynchronous questions, reflections, or discussions [N1-F1][N2-F2].  

The evidence does not provide a fully detailed protocol for every type of interaction, but it does support a clear pattern: **the role model leads the live, synchronous part of the visit, while participants lead the asynchronous follow-up and reflection** [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### 3) How timing, scheduling, and pacing differ across modes

The hybrid model is especially valuable because it addresses differences in timing, scheduling, and pacing.  

- **Synchronous interaction** requires participants to be present at predetermined times, which can create scheduling constraints [N2-F2].  
- **Asynchronous interaction**, by contrast, allows participants to engage at their own pace, improving flexibility and access [N2-F2].  
- The virtual role model visit literature also notes that digital technologies can save resources in terms of transport and planning and that visits can be scaled to reach more pupils and make better use of the role models’ time [N1-F1]. This implies that synchronous sessions are often scheduled to maximize direct engagement, while asynchronous components are paced to accommodate broader participation and repeated engagement over time [N1-F1][N2-F2].  

### 4) Advantages of hybrid projects for virtual role model visits

The main advantages of hybrid projects are that they combine **accessibility, immediacy, and reflection** into one model.

#### a) Flexibility improves participation and access

Asynchronous components reduce scheduling burden by allowing participants to engage at their own pace, which is especially helpful when participants have nontraditional schedules, family responsibilities, or geographic constraints [N2-F2]. The broader hybrid-learning literature notes that asynchronous learning allows anyone, anywhere to participate and eliminates the barrier of time zones [N2-F2]. In the virtual role model visit context, this means the model can reach students in sparsely populated areas and connect them with role models who might otherwise be inaccessible [N1-F1].  

#### b) Real-time interaction supports immediacy and rapport

Synchronous interaction supports immediacy and rapport by enabling direct communication, questions, clarifications, and group discussions during a visit [N2-F2]. The virtual role model visit literature explicitly notes that digital technologies can improve the interaction with the “real world,” including role models, by technology-mediated engagement [N1-F1]. It also states that role models can show authentic work tasks and environments through virtual field visits, which strengthens the presence and authenticity of the role model experience [N1-F1].  

#### c) Asynchronous components reduce scheduling burden and enable reflection

Asynchronous learning eliminates the need for all participants to be present at the same time, which makes it easier to accommodate multiple participants across different time zones or conflicting schedules [N2-F2]. At the same time, asynchronous formats allow learners to review material, process it, and reflect more deeply before engaging further [N2-F2]. In the virtual role model visit context, this is especially relevant because participants can later reflect on the role model’s work tasks and environments after the live session [N1-F1].  

### 5) Limitations and tradeoffs

Hybrid projects also introduce important limitations and tradeoffs that should be acknowledged.

#### a) Potential fragmentation or confusion from mixed modes

The general hybrid-learning literature notes that strictly asynchronous learning can reduce a learner’s ability to engage, build peer relationships, and work collaboratively, and that group projects become largely solo endeavors in asynchronous spaces [N2-F2]. In the virtual role model visit context, this could translate into participants being pulled between different interaction modes without clear boundaries, which may make the visit feel disjointed or harder to follow [N2-F2]. The virtual role model visit literature also emphasizes that digital technologies enable interaction through both synchronous and asynchronous communication, which implies that the hybrid design must be carefully structured to avoid confusion about what is expected when [N1-F1].  

#### b) Technical barriers to seamless switching or integration

Technical barriers can complicate the hybrid model. The hybrid-learning evidence notes that hybrid models combine real-time and at-your-own-pace experiences, but it also highlights that scheduling conflicts and reliance on real-time communication without asynchronous resources can create gaps and missed learning opportunities [N2-F2]. In virtual role model visits, this could mean participants may struggle with technical transitions between modes, such as moving from a live Q&A session to a recorded follow-up or asynchronous reflection task, especially if the platform or workflow is not well integrated [N2-F2]. The logistics and implementation evidence from the broader hybrid-learning context also points to the need for structured organization and clear planning when mixing live and digital learning [N4-R1]. While that evidence is broader, it supports the idea that technical integration can be a bottleneck rather than a straightforward benefit [N4-R1].  

#### c) Participant workload and attention may change

Participant workload and attention can also change in ways that are not always positive. The hybrid-learning literature states that synchronous learning can only happen at predetermined times, so scheduling conflicts may cause participants to miss opportunities [N2-F2]. Asynchronous learning, while flexible, can also increase workload because participants may need to manage more self-directed work, review materials, and wait for clarifications through email or messaging [N2-F2]. In the virtual role model visit context, this means participants may face a heavier cognitive load: they must attend a live session, then later process and reflect on the content asynchronously, while also managing the extra work of staying on task and keeping up with the visit’s requirements [N2-F2].  

### 6) Context-specific evidence for role model visits in virtual settings

The evidence supports virtual role model visits especially well in **education and coaching contexts**, with the strongest support coming from STEM education and professional development settings.

#### a) Which settings are most suited to this model?

- **Education settings**: The virtual role model visit literature focuses on students’ encounters with STEM role models and notes that digital technologies enable scaling so that more young people can have access to role models [N1-F1]. It also states that role models can show authentic work tasks and environments through virtual field visits, which makes the model especially suitable for STEM outreach and youth engagement [N1-F1].  
- **Coaching and mentoring settings**: Virtual mentoring and coaching literature frames VMC as an effective method to support teachers and other professionals in professional development [N5-F3]. It also describes VMC as a viable alternative when traditional methods are unfeasible, and as a way to provide individualized support through web-based, online, or e-mentoring/coaching formats [N5-F3].  
- **Professional development settings**: The virtual mentoring and coaching review emphasizes that structured mentoring programs encourage teamwork, leadership, and research, helping teachers enhance their approaches and remain effective [N5-R5]. This supports the use of virtual role model visits in coaching and professional development contexts where guidance, reflection, and support are central [N5-F3][N5-R5].  

#### b) Outcomes supported by the evidence

The evidence supports several outcomes:  
- **Improved access and reach**: Virtual role model visits can scale to reach more pupils, especially in sparsely populated areas, and can connect students with a diversity of role models [N1-F1].  
- **Improved motivation and engagement**: The virtual role model visit literature states that digital technologies can strengthen young people’s motivation to pursue a STEM education by exposing them to workplace professionals and authentic work environments [N1-F1].  
- **Improved professional development and support**: Virtual mentoring and coaching literature finds that VMC is an effective method to support teachers, and that it can be efficient in feasibility and accessibility without negatively impacting its effectiveness [N5-F3].  
- **Improved reflection and follow-up**: Asynchronous components allow participants to review, reflect, and process the visit at their own pace [N2-F2][N1-F1].  

#### c) Evidence gaps and exceptions

The evidence should be interpreted cautiously.  
- The virtual mentoring and coaching evidence indicates **variability in implementation design**, making it difficult to pinpoint which specific features make VMC effective [N5-F3].  
- The virtual role model visit literature review excludes studies that only briefly mention digital technology rather than using it as a communication tool between role models and young people, which means the evidence base is still evolving and not yet fully standardized [N1-F1].  
- The evidence is **stronger in STEM education and professional development contexts** than in all coaching or role model settings, so generalization should be cautious [N1-F1][N5-F3].  

### 7) Bottom line

Hybrid projects in virtual role model visits are best understood as a **balanced design** that integrates **live, synchronous interaction** with **self-paced, asynchronous follow-up** [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The advantages are substantial:  
- **Flexibility** improves participation and access, especially for students with nontraditional schedules or geographic constraints [N2-F2].  
- **Real-time interaction** supports immediacy, rapport, and authentic engagement with role models [N1-F1][N2-F2].
